events.text: At the spring fair, a child from the next village beats you at every game, and then, handing back your winnings, says shyly that you are the best they have ever lost to. {npc} is nine years old and has your exact way of scowling.

ok.log: You beat {npc} at the stone-and-string, the last game of the day, and the whole fair turns to watch. {He} shakes your hand like a grown-up, hard.

fail.log: You lose the stone-and-string, the last game, and {npc} gives you the winnings back anyway, which is worse.

effects.log: You split the winnings with {npc}, and spend them together on honey cakes. It is the start of something odd.

events.text: {npc} is waiting at the ford where the two villages meet, with a long stick, saying that the boy and girl on this side have to prove who is faster across. {He} does not say how {he} knows you are coming. It is as if you had arranged it long ago.

ok.log: You cross first, wet to the knees, and {npc} scowls and then laughs, and wades across behind you.

fail.log: You slip in the middle, and {npc} reaches the far bank first and, with a ruffled air, throws you the stick to pull yourself out.

effects.log: You wade across together, arguing the whole way, and meet your mothers on the bank, who exchange a strange, long look.

events.text: The teacher of the fighting arts in the market town takes two new pupils in the same week: you, and {npc}. The teacher sets you against each other in the first lesson, with wooden staves, and watches with a pleased, unreadable face.

ok.log: You win the first bout, narrowly, and {npc} bows, rigidly, and says "Again, tomorrow," and means it.

fail.log: You lose the first bout, narrowly, and {npc} bows, rigidly, and says "Again, tomorrow," and means it.

choices.text: Ask the teacher to pair you differently

effects.log: The teacher refuses, kindly, and says some things are not chosen. You spar with {npc} anyway, and learn more than the others.

events.text: The two villages hold a footrace at harvest, a custom nobody can explain, and {npc} has trained all summer. {He} stands at the line beside you, panting with nerves, and mutters, "I do not want to lose to you. I do not know why."

ok.log: You win the race by a nose, and {npc} stands at the finish line with {his} hands on {his} knees, laughing, for no reason.

fail.log: You lose the race by a nose, and {npc} falls on the grass, wheezing, and offers you a hand up.

effects.log: You run beside {npc}, matching pace, and cross together. The judges argue about it until dark.

events.text: A travelling storyteller tells of two heroes of old who were born on the same night and fought all their lives. {npc} sits at the back of the crowd, and when the tale is over looks across at you, and the two of you are the only ones who do not clap.

ok.log: You find {npc} afterwards at the well and challenge {him} to a staff-match to settle which of you is the hero. You win, and neither of you feels like a hero.

fail.log: You find {npc} afterwards at the well, and {he} challenges you. {He} wins, and offers a drink from the bucket, and says nothing.

effects.log: "That it was sad," says {npc}. "Both of them." You nod, and the two of you sit by the well till the lamps are lit.

events.text: In the lean year, the harvest is poor on both sides of the river, and a dispute over the wells brings the two villages to the bridge. {npc} stands at the head of the other crowd, and you at the head of yours, and the bridge is very narrow.

ok.log: You stand your ground at the bridge, and the other side gives way, grumbling, and {npc} nods to you, once, as to an equal.

fail.log: You are pushed back at the bridge, and your side loses the well, and {npc} looks at you with a faint, unhappy pity.

effects.log: You propose to share, and the elders are shocked, and then relieved. {npc} says the idea was theirs, and it is almost true.

events.text: A bandit gang has been preying on the road between your villages, and a notice goes up asking for brave people to guard the next caravan. Two names are on it by the next morning: yours and {npc}'s. You have not spoken for a year.

choices.text: Guard the front of the caravan

ok.log: You hold the road, and the bandits turn back, and {npc} is beside you at the end with a split lip and a grin.

fail.log: The bandits break through on your side, and {npc} covers the gap, and neither of you says a word of it afterwards.

choices.text: Go together, and agree on a plan

effects.log: You agree on a plan over a bowl of noodles, and for the first time you each hear what the other would do. It works.

events.text: The Maker's festival comes round, and every village brings a lantern to float on the river. {npc} has made a very bad one. It leaks, and leans, and {he} has not noticed, and is carrying it with pride. The crowd is beginning to smile.

ok.log: You help, secretly, and your hands steady the lantern while {npc} is not looking. It floats, and {he} gasps, and looks round for the one who helped.

fail.log: You try to help, and the lantern goes down in a hiss, and {npc} turns and sees you holding it, and says, "Well, thank you for that," in a very small voice.

effects.log: You float yours beside theirs. They are very different lanterns, and the river carries both.

events.text: A fever goes round both villages in the spring, and the healer is overwhelmed. You find {npc} at your door at dusk with a basket of herbs, a drawn face, and a sentence that clearly cost {him} an hour to prepare: "I know it is not what we do, but I would like to help."

ok.log: You work all night beside {npc}, sorting and brewing, and by dawn the worst is over, and both of you have fallen asleep sitting up.

fail.log: You work beside {npc}, and the fever takes hold of you at last, and {he} carries you home through the dawn, grumbling.

choices.text: Accept the herbs, and thank them

effects.log: You thank {npc}. {He} turns scarlet, and puts the basket down, and leaves very fast.

events.text: The two of you are chosen, by the quirk of a village lottery, to carry the Maker's banner to the hill shrine for the new year. It is a long climb. The banner is heavy. {npc} says nothing for the first hour, and then, panting, "We could take turns."

choices.text: Carry the banner the hard way

ok.log: You take the steep stretch, and {npc} the long one, and the banner reaches the shrine, and neither of you will say who carried it.

fail.log: You tire first, and {npc} takes the banner, and says nothing at all about it, and you resent the silence.

effects.log: You take turns. The climb is long and the talk is longer, and by the shrine you have said more to {npc} than to anyone in your life.

events.text: Every autumn the two villages hold a tug-of-rope across the stream, and every year the same two people end up at the front: you, and {npc}. This year the rope is old and the stream is high, and the crowd is larger than anyone has seen.

choices.text: Pull for all you are worth

ok.log: You pull, and the rope holds, and the other side goes into the stream in a heap, and {npc} comes up spluttering and laughing, and reaches out a wet hand.

fail.log: You pull, and the rope holds, and then it does not, and you go into the stream, and {npc} stands on the bank and, helplessly, offers a towel.

effects.log: You let go on purpose, and the whole of the other side goes into the stream, and {npc} looks at you from the water with the face of a person who has been robbed and relieved.

events.text: A travelling company of players sets up in the market, and one of the plays is about two rivals, and the people watching are the two of you. The players play it well enough that {npc} shifts in {his} seat, and mutters, "That is not how it went."

ok.log: You stand up in the middle of the play and say how it went. The crowd laughs, then falls silent, and the players, startled, let you finish. {npc} claps first.

fail.log: You stand up and try to correct the play, and are laughed down, and {npc} pulls you back into your seat by the sleeve.

effects.log: You watch to the end. The play finishes badly for both heroes. {npc} wipes {his} eyes and says, "Well, that is that, then."

events.text: At the fair of the autumn crossroads, there is a contest of arms open to anyone, and the two of you are on the same side of the board. The draw has been kind, or unkind. Only one of you can reach the last round.

ok.log: You win the bout against {npc}, and {he} congratulates you with such grace that you almost wish you had lost.

fail.log: You lose the bout against {npc}, and {he} lifts your arm as you leave, for the crowd to see, and it is somehow worse.

effects.log: You concede, and wish them luck. {npc} goes on to the last round and loses, and says that you should have fought.

events.text: A great storm takes the roof off the mill that both villages use, and in the morning the wreckage lies across the road. {npc} is already there, hauling beams, and waves for you to take the other end. "I will not be argued with," says {he}. "Lift."

ok.log: You lift, and the beam comes up, and the road is cleared by noon, and you are both too tired to quarrel.

fail.log: You lift, and the beam slips, and {npc} takes the weight on one shoulder and swears at you, in a very small voice, so as not to alarm the children.

choices.text: Say you are busy, and go

effects.log: You say you are busy, and go. It is a very poor thing to have done, and you carry it the whole day.

events.text: The lamplighter's daughter in the next village falls ill, and the only physician within a week's walk is in your town. {npc} arrives at your door at midnight, breathless, to ask whether you would speak for {him}, because the physician does not know {him} and does know you.

choices.text: Go to the physician with them

ok.log: You speak for {npc}, and the physician comes, and the child lives. {npc} says nothing, and sends a small carved bird the next spring.

fail.log: You speak for {npc}, but the physician is stubborn, and the child is saved by other means, and {npc} thanks you anyway, and means it.

effects.log: You give the address. {npc} is gone before you can say more, and you wonder for years what you would have said.

events.text: You find {npc} in the loft of the old barn between your villages, hiding from something. It turns out to be a letter, from home, that {he} cannot bring {his} hands to open. "I thought," says {npc}, "that you of all people would understand."

ok.log: You read it together. It is good news, in a bad hand, and {npc} laughs until {he} cries, and you laugh with {him}.

fail.log: You read it together. It is bad news, and {npc} sits very quietly for a long time, and you stay beside {him}.

effects.log: You leave them the barn. It is the kindest thing you can think of, and you wonder if it was.

events.text: A boy from the neighbouring village has been insulting you in the market, and {npc} walks up to the boy, calmly, and tells the boy to stop. "That one is mine to be rude to," says {npc}, "and you do it badly." The crowd is delighted. You are not sure if you have been defended.

choices.text: Challenge them to settle it, then and there

ok.log: You thank {npc}, and {he} shrugs it off, and the next week you defend {him} in return, and neither of you refers to either occasion.

fail.log: You thank {npc}, and {he} says "It was nothing," in a way that suggests it was a very great deal, and you stand there embarrassed.

effects.log: You thank {npc}. {He} turns pink, and says "Do not make a habit of it," and goes.

events.text: The Maker's shrine at the crossroads has a custom: two petitioners praying for the same thing must share the offering. You and {npc} have come, on the same morning, to ask for the same rain. The priest looks from one to the other with an expression of deep, kind amusement.

ok.log: You offer first, and the rain comes in the afternoon, and the priest says that the Maker favours the bold, which is not, in fact, an old saying.

fail.log: You offer second, and the rain comes in the afternoon anyway, to the great relief of the priest, who has no theology prepared for this.

choices.text: Offer together, out of the same bowl

effects.log: You offer together. The priest weeps a little. The rain comes, and so do other things.

events.text: Years on, {npc} and you are both asked to take a place at the head of the guild of fighting arts in the great town, but there is only one place. The guild has a custom: the matter is decided by a single bout, at dawn, with the whole town watching.

ok.log: You win the dawn bout, and the town cheers, and {npc} bows, and says "Well fought," in a voice that has no bitterness, which is what you will remember.

fail.log: You lose the dawn bout, and the town cheers, and you bow, and say "Well fought," and mean it, and are surprised how much.

choices.text: Refuse the place, and recommend them

effects.log: You refuse, and recommend them. The guild is astonished. {npc} comes to your door that night and does not say anything for a long time.

events.text: A fire starts in the grain store of the town, and in the confusion you find {npc} on the roof, with a bucket, shouting for more hands. Without thinking, you climb up beside {him}. The two of you stand in the smoke, with the whole town below.

ok.log: You hold the fire back until the bucket line arrives, and the grain is saved, and the two of you are hauled down black with soot, to a roar from the crowd.

fail.log: The fire takes the roof, but the two of you get the people out, and the grain is lost, and you sit on the kerb with {npc}, coughing, and say nothing.

effects.log: You pull {him} down. {He} fights you, and then does not, and the roof falls where you stood.

events.text: Someone has chalked a rude rhyme about the two of you on the wall of the school, and the children are chanting it. {npc} reads it aloud, in front of them, in a flat voice. "It does not even scan," says {he}. "I will teach you a better one."

choices.text: Write a better rhyme than theirs

ok.log: You and {npc} write a better rhyme together, on the same wall, in bright chalk, and the children learn it by evening, and it is about the two of you, kindly.

fail.log: You and {npc} try to write a better rhyme. It is no better. The children chant both, and the town hums them for a month.

effects.log: You rub out the wall, with {npc}'s sleeve and yours. Underneath is an older rhyme, and a smaller one, and it is kind.

events.text: The ferryman who knew the Maker, they say, sits at the crossing, and you and {npc} are brought to the old man by the same errand. The ferryman studies you both for a long time. "You are knotted," says the ferryman. "I would cut it, if I were you. Or tie it better." That is all the ferryman will say.

choices.text: Say you will tie it better

ok.log: You say you will tie it better. {npc} says the same, at the same moment, and you both stare at the water for a while, unsettled.

fail.log: You say you will cut it. {npc} says nothing at all, and the ferryman nods, slowly, as if something had been written down.

choices.text: Ask the ferryman what that means

effects.log: "Ask the Maker," says the ferryman. "Do not ask me." The ferryman rows away, and the two of you stand there, thinking.

events.text: {npc} comes to your door at the end of a long life, with grey hair and a stick, and says: "I have been your rival for every year of it. I would like to stop. If you wish it, I will put down every grudge. If you do not, I will understand." {He} holds out an open hand.

choices.text: Take their hand, and end it

effects.log: You take it. The grip is dry and warm and shaking. Something that has been tight in you since you were a child lets go.
You refuse, and what follows is a last, slow, honest match in the yard. When it is over, the thing between you has a finish.
You ask for a season. {npc} nods and gives it, and neither of you knows what you will say.

events.text: On the last day of the harvest, {npc} comes to the field where you are working and kneels, stiffly, in the stubble. "I yield," {he} says. "Not because you are stronger. Because I am tired of being the one who is never quite enough." {He} looks up. "Will you take it?"

effects.log: You raise them up, and say that there was never a contest, only two people from two villages, and {npc} weeps into your sleeve.
You accept. The weight of it settles on you like snow. It is a victory and it is not at all what you wanted.
You decline to take it, and decline to give it back, and the matter stays unsettled, and warm.

events.text: {npc} says that the knot between you is thin now, worn almost through by use. {He} asks whether you would prefer to cut it, with a clean stroke, or let it fray, and carry what remains, as a friend, for the rest of your lives.

choices.text: Let it be, and carry it

effects.log: You let it be. It frays slowly, and years later you find it has become something like a bridge.
You cut it. The silence afterwards is the cleanest you have ever heard, and the loneliest, and entirely your own.
You say neither. {npc} smiles, and the knot hums, and both of you pretend not to hear.

events.text: At the end of a salt road no one maps, you find {b3_legend} sitting very still on a post, watching a line of camels go by. They do not look up. The silence is of the kind that has been practised for years, and is not, you realise, an insult.

effects.log: You sit. An hour passes, then a day. When you rise, you have been taught something, though you could not say what.

choices.text: Ask the one question you have

effects.log: You ask. The answer is five words, and it will take you thirty years to understand all of them.
You bow and go. The legend lifts one finger, perhaps a blessing, perhaps a fly. You will never know.

events.text: Everyone has a story about {b3_legend}, and no two agree. You find them in a roadside inn, quite alive, arguing mildly with a kettle about its temperature. The kettle is losing.

effects.log: You take the kettle's side. The legend is delighted. The afternoon is long, and unexpectedly useful.

choices.text: Ask which of the stories is true

effects.log: "All of them," says the legend, "in their fashion. Pour me some more."
You pay. The legend accepts with great seriousness, as if the payment were the point of the visit. Perhaps it was.

events.text: {b3_legend} sees you across a crowded market and crosses the square to you, ignoring three merchants and a magistrate. "You," they say. "I have been meaning to look at you." They look for a very long time.

effects.log: You hold it. The look goes on, and on, and then ends, and the legend says only "Good", and walks away, leaving the merchants in your debt.

choices.text: Look back, and ask what they see

effects.log: "A very slow fuse," says the legend. "Lit." They are gone before you can ask more.
You bow low. The legend grunts. It is, as far as the market can tell, an endorsement.

events.text: On the seventh bridge, {b3_legend} is dropping pebbles into the river one at a time, and listening. "There," they say, as you come up. "That one went a long way down. Did you hear?" You did not, but you listen.

effects.log: You drop one. The legend cocks their head. "Not bad," they say. "You have the ear for it."
"For when it stops," they say. "It never does. That is the secret. Do not tell anyone."
You stand beside them. After an hour the legend sighs, contentedly, and you feel something in you set down a load.

events.text: The cottage door is open and the garden swept. Inside, {b3_legend} is scrubbing a table that looks as if it had never been dirty. They look up and say, "Thank goodness, someone to hold the other end," and hand you a cloth.

effects.log: You scrub. It takes three days. At the end the legend inspects the table, and nods, and you have the odd sense of having passed an examination.
"Because somebody must," says the legend, and leaves it at that, and it stays with you for thirty years.
You decline the cloth, with an apology. The legend smiles, takes it, and goes on scrubbing, quite unoffended.

events.text: You meet {b3_legend} at a ferry landing, both of you waiting for a boat that has not come in a season. They tell you it is coming, with such confidence that you begin to feel it too.

effects.log: You wait. Nothing arrives. But the waiting has a shape, and the shape is a lesson in patience of the kind that cannot be hurried.

choices.text: Ask what they are waiting for

effects.log: "For the next thing," they say. "It is always the next thing." You write it down, and cannot read the note later.
You offer to row, and the legend laughs until they have to sit, and accepts, and you row the whole afternoon, round and round in sunlight.

events.text: {b3_legend} challenges you to a contest of silence, a strange match, with a single secret each as the prize. You are curious enough to accept. The contest lasts three days.

choices.text: Hold the silence to the end

ok.log: You hold it, and in the end it is the legend who speaks first, and gives you the secret, kindly.

fail.log: You break first, and the legend takes your secret with a very gentle expression.

effects.log: You concede at once. The legend is a little disappointed, a little pleased, and tells you a smaller secret, as a consolation.
You offer a draw, and the legend, to the astonishment of three listening children, accepts.

events.text: You find {b3_legend} asleep under a pear tree on a very small hill, snoring gently, and the tree is shedding blossom all over them. You are not sure whether to wake them. A single petal falls on your sleeve, and it is warm.

effects.log: The legend wakes, blinks, and says, "Ah, you again," as if you had met every spring. It is a pleasant lie, and you are not sure it is one.
You sit. The petals fall. When the legend wakes at last, you are a little calmer than you were.

choices.text: Leave a cup of water beside them

effects.log: You leave a cup. It is cold when they wake, and they drink it anyway, and the gesture is repaid, in time.

events.text: The gate of a small farm opens before you, and {b3_legend} is in the yard, looking at the sky. "I have been told," they say, "that you are a person who gets to the point. Get to the point."

effects.log: You say it plainly. The legend nods, and tells you the one thing you needed, and a second, free of charge.

choices.text: Say you have come to learn

effects.log: You say you have come to learn. The legend sighs, "Ah. Everyone says that," and teaches you anyway.

choices.text: Say you only came to see

effects.log: You say you only came to see. The legend roars with laughter, and for the rest of the afternoon you are a guest.

events.text: Rain, the first in a long season, falls on a tiny shrine to the Maker at the edge of a field, and {b3_legend} sits in the doorway, watching it, with the look of someone seeing an old friend. They gesture you in, out of the wet.

choices.text: Sit in the doorway beside them

effects.log: You sit beside them. The rain falls for two days, and nothing is said, and it is the best conversation of your life.

choices.text: Ask whether they remember a rain like it

effects.log: "There was one," says the legend, "and I was not the same after." That is all, and it is a great deal.
You go. The rain follows you down the lane for an hour, and then it clears.

events.text: A very small dispute, over a toll of one coin at a plank bridge, has gone to {b3_legend} for judgement, and they have been hearing it for three days. They look at you, a passing traveller, and say, "You. You decide." Both parties turn.

effects.log: You rule for the toll-keeper. The traveller grumbles, pays, and then, at the last, grins. The legend nods, and says that is the kind of thing that makes a bridge.
You rule for the traveller. The toll-keeper takes it with grace, and the legend says, mildly, "Interesting."
You make them share. Both are unsatisfied. Both go away to tell it as a victory. The legend says that is the best kind of justice.

events.text: You find {b3_legend} in a garden of white stones, rearranging them with infinite care, one by one. Every so often they step back and look, and move one a hair to the left. You realise they have been doing this for years.

effects.log: You move one. The legend considers it for a long time and moves it back, a hair to the right, and says, "Better." You do not see the difference. You will, in thirty years.

choices.text: Ask what the garden is for

effects.log: "For being a garden," they say, without turning. "That is all any of us are for."
You sit and watch. You watch for three days. At the end of it, the garden looks the same, and you do not.

events.text: {b3_legend} stops you on the road, with a hand on your sleeve, and says, quite seriously: "You are about to make a mistake. A large one. I cannot say what. I only wanted to say that I will not think less of you."

effects.log: You thank them, and take extra care for a year, and the mistake, when it comes, is smaller than it would have been.
"I do not know," says the legend. "I am only old, not clever." You have never been so reassured.
You go on, regardless, and make the mistake, and the legend, when you next meet, says nothing about it, and that is the kindest thing.

events.text: There is an old custom in the villages: to meet {b3_legend}, you must come with something to give and nothing to ask. You arrive with a loaf of plain bread, and the legend looks at it for a long time.

effects.log: The legend takes the bread, and eats it, slowly, and says it is the best they have had. It is not, but they mean it as a kind of blessing.

choices.text: Ask if they would like something else

effects.log: You ask. They say bread is the right thing, and you are the first to bring it in thirty years.

choices.text: Keep the bread, and give nothing

effects.log: You keep the bread. The legend watches you, and says "Ah," in a tone that is not unkind, and does not say what it means.

events.text: At the market of a very small town, somebody tells you that {b3_legend} has been seen haggling over a bag of dried plums with the vigour of a young merchant. You go. It is true. They are winning.

effects.log: You help. The legend and you take the merchant for a good deal of plums, and share them on a wall, and it is a fine afternoon.
You haggle against them. It is a close fight, and a dear one, and the merchant goes home with a very good story.
You buy the plums. The legend takes them, solemnly, and bows. "I will remember the plums," they say. You hope so.

events.text: The one whose fate is knotted to yours has had a bad winter, and you know it the way you know the weather. A neighbour would say it was nothing to do with you. Something in you says it is. You find yourself sending a small gift, without a name.

effects.log: You send it. It is received, and traced, and neither of you mentions it, and the knot between you hums quietly.
You hold it back. The pride is old and the habit older. You will think of it on the road, for a long time.

choices.text: Send it with your name on it

effects.log: You send it with your name. The reply is three lines, and the third is a joke, which is the best thing it could have been.

events.text: There is someone in the next village who looks at you, at the fair, as if you were a word on the tip of their tongue. You have the same feeling in return. Neither of you has ever spoken of it. This year, for no reason, you find yourself saying hello.

effects.log: You say hello properly. It is the beginning of a conversation that will last, on and off, for many years.
You nod and go on. It is very correct, and it is a small, odd grief.

choices.text: Ask if they, too, feel it

effects.log: You ask. They look at you with huge, startled eyes, and say "Yes."

events.text: You wake with a name in your mouth that you do not know, and by evening you learn that someone with that name has been made the head of a guild, and you are, to your shame, a little jealous. You do not know them. You are quite sure you know them.

effects.log: You send it. The reply comes by return, and says only: "Thank you. I felt that."
You work harder, for no reason you can name, and in the morning you are a little better than you were.
You pretend. It is a very poor pretence, and you carry it all week.

events.text: A fortune-teller at the autumn fair says, without being asked, that you and someone you have not yet met are "an old song sung in two keys". You ask who. She cannot say. She only says to be kind, when the time comes.

effects.log: You promise. She looks relieved, and rather sad, and gives you a very small coin, for luck.

choices.text: Ask what happens if you are not

effects.log: "Then you will do it again," she says. "It is the only rule."

choices.text: Say you do not believe in songs

effects.log: You say so, loudly. She smiles, very kindly, as one smiles at a child.

events.text: The old unaccountable ache has come back, the one that surfaces in the second week of the autumn rains: that someone is walking behind you on the road, a step back, and has been for years. You turn. There is nobody. There is a lantern, swinging on a post.

effects.log: You wait. For an hour, then two. Nobody comes. But the waiting is a small, warm thing, and you carry it home.
You walk on faster. Behind you the lantern swings, and the road, for a moment, seems to hold its breath.

choices.text: Call out a name you do not know

effects.log: You call a name. The wind brings it back to you. It is, you realise, your own, in somebody else's voice.

events.text: At a wedding feast in the market town you have a sense that the one whose fate follows yours is in the room, and you scan every face. A stranger at the far table meets your eyes and holds them. Neither of you looks away for a very long time.

effects.log: You cross the room. It takes a long time, and a great deal of nerve, and at the end there is a very ordinary introduction, and a very unordinary silence.
You raise your cup. They raise theirs. That is all. It is a great deal.
You look away. It is a small cowardice, and you will remember it, and the next time you meet, you will not.

events.text: Someone leaves a spray of plum blossom on your sill in the night, every year, on the same night. You have never seen them. This year you wait up, and in the small hours a shadow comes, and stops, and sees you, and does not run.

effects.log: You say it. The shadow says "You are welcome," and then, rather quietly, "You always say that."
"I do not know," says the shadow. "I only know that I have to." It is, you realise, the truest answer you have heard.
You offer. They sit, awkwardly, in the one good chair, and the two of you are quiet for a very long time.

events.text: When you were young, a stranger on the road said, "I will see you again, whatever happens." You had forgotten. Today, at a crossroads, a pair of eyes meets yours, and a voice from long ago says, softly, "There."

choices.text: Answer, as if you had been waiting

effects.log: You answer. It is the only thing you can do, and it is entirely right, and the rest of the year is never quite the same.
You say you do not. The stranger says, "No. But I will wait." It is an unkind kind of kindness.
You walk past, and your hands do not stop shaking until midnight.

events.text: A pedlar sells you a small clay whistle at the fair and says that it is a "two-note whistle", and that its twin has been sold to someone in the next village. You blow it. Far off, faintly, an answering note comes back, and then a laugh.

effects.log: You blow it again. The answer comes again, and the two of you play a ridiculous, tuneless duet across a mile of fields for a quarter of an hour.
You put it away. On quiet nights you hear it, faintly, in the drawer.
You go looking. It takes a week, and the other turns out to be a child of eleven, and the answer is a long story.

events.text: You and someone from the next village are both named in the will of an old teacher you each thought you alone had loved. The will says: "Settle it between you." The two of you meet at the teacher's grave with a most embarrassed civility.

effects.log: You split it exactly, to the last button, and the exactness is almost an insult, and almost a kindness.
You give it all to them. They give it all back. After an hour of that, you give up and go to the inn, and share the lot over supper.

choices.text: Ask them to tell you about the teacher

effects.log: You ask. They talk for hours, and it is a different teacher, and the same one, and you part friends of a sort.

events.text: The Maker's festival comes, and for the first time you and the one fated to you find yourselves side by side in the long line to the shrine. You do not look at each other. At the door the priest offers one blessing for two, and you reach for it together.

effects.log: You take it together. The priest smiles, as if he had arranged it, which he had not.
You let them have it. They let you have it. The priest, patient, waits.
You break it in half, between you, like bread. It is a small thing to do. It is not a small thing.

events.text: A letter arrives with no name, only a drawing of a pair of sparrows on a wire. You do not know who sent it. You know, anyway. You have never in your life drawn a sparrow, but you find yourself reaching for a pen.

effects.log: You draw a reply. It is a poor drawing of a single sparrow, and you send it to a place you do not know the way to, and it arrives.
You keep the letter, in a drawer you open on quiet nights.
You burn it. The smoke goes up in the shape of nothing in particular, and you feel strangely lighter and strangely robbed.

events.text: There is a night each year when the two of you, in your two houses, a long way apart, find you cannot sleep. You each sit up, and trim a lamp, and look at the window. On this night, you realise, you are each doing it for the other. You light a second lamp.

effects.log: You leave it burning until dawn. Across the fields, you are almost sure, another lamp does the same.

choices.text: Walk out to meet them halfway

effects.log: You walk out into the dark. At the stile, a shape is waiting, and says, "I thought you might." You sit on the stile till morning.

choices.text: Blow out both lamps and sleep

effects.log: You blow out both lamps and sleep, badly, and wake with the feeling of having missed an appointment.

events.text: In the market of the town on the river, you see a face in a crowd that you have never seen before, and every part of you says "There you are." You push through. By the time you reach the spot they have gone. A single coin lies on the cobbles, warm.

effects.log: You pick it up, and keep it, and it is never quite cold again.

choices.text: Ask the stallholders who it was

effects.log: They shrug. One says, "Oh, that one. Always in a hurry. Always looks back." You find that you have been looking back too.

choices.text: Wait at the spot for an hour

effects.log: You wait an hour. They do not come. You feel, rather than see, that they too are waiting, somewhere else, at their own spot.

events.text: You have kept, without knowing why, a small blue button that you found in the road when you were seven. This year a stranger at the fair holds out a hand with a sleeve that has one button missing, and the missing button is blue. Neither of you says anything for a long moment.

effects.log: You hand it over. The stranger sews it on at once, with a needle from a hat, and the two of you stand in the road, looking at a sleeve.

choices.text: Ask where they got the sleeve

effects.log: "My mother made it," says the stranger. "Out of something she could not remember." You have the same words ready, and do not use them.

choices.text: Keep the button, and say nothing

effects.log: You keep the button. The stranger goes on, buttonless, and looks back once. You will wonder, for a good many years.
